title: Certified Phenom Instructor exam
rulesHtml:
Certified Phenom Instructor exam

Forty questions in three parts. Sixty minutes. Pass with 32 of 40 and no part below its floor.

Before you start

  • When to take it. On demand, after Lesson 20, when the drills in Lessons 9, 15 and 16 feel calm.
  • Time. 60 minutes for all three parts. Work in any order.
  • What you may use. Your abacus for Parts A and B. A pencil and this paper. Nothing else.
  • What you may not use. A calculator, the trainer, the course notes, or another person. Question 24 is mental: no abacus and no paper for that one.
  • How to answer. Part A: name the move and write its spoken line. Part B: write the answer (and, for 25 and 26, every rod move in order). Part C: circle one letter.

How it is marked

PartWhat it testsQuestionsFloor
ABead-move classification1–129 of 12
BWorked problems13–2610 of 14
CTeaching scenarios27–4010 of 14
AllPass mark4032 of 40 (80%)

One point per question. No half points. You pass when your total is 32 or more and every part meets its floor. If you miss, you get your score for each part and can retake whenever you are ready, on a fresh form. After a second miss, the Pass Promise starts: one-on-one coaching until you pass.

parts.title: Bead moves
parts.introHtml: The ones rod shows the first number. The tens rod has room to carry and beads to lend. For each one, name the move (free beads, small friend, big friend, or both friends at once), write it as a formula, and write the line a child says.

parts.title: Worked problems
parts.introHtml: Work each problem left to right. Write only the answer, except 25 and 26.

questions.text: A mom says, "His doctor wants to try ADHD medicine. Could the abacus work instead?" What do you say?

options.label: "The founder had ADHD and did great with the beads, so try them first and keep the medicine as a backup."
"That's for his doctor to decide. The beads aren't a treatment. They build arithmetic speed and accuracy."
"The beads calm busy kids, so he may not need the medicine."
"Many families use the beads instead of medicine. Give it a month first, and then see how he does at school."

questions.text: A Stage 3 boy works 28 + 7 and writes 25. What do you say?

options.label: "What's the friend of seven? Say it, then do the move again."
"Start on the ones rod this time, then move to the tens rod."
"It's 35. Watch me do it once, then you try the next one."
"Take away the friend, then carry one to the left."

questions.text: A Stage 1 girl pushes earth beads up with her index finger. What do you do?

options.label: Hold her thumb and move the beads with it for her.
Let it go, since her answers are right.
Explain how each finger works before every problem.
Say "Thumb for up," then move on.

questions.text: It is 8 p.m. A child is tired and cranky. The Apprentice boss is planned for tonight. What do you tell the parent?

options.label: "Let her take it twice tonight, so that one bad try doesn't count against her."
"Give her a hint or two, so she can pass and get to bed."
"Not tonight. A tired child should not take a boss. Try it on a fresh day."
"Go ahead. A little pressure at bedtime helps her focus on the clock."

questions.text: A girl has cleared rung 15 of the Bead Score. Her mom asks you to write "1st kyu" on her progress report. What do you write?

options.label: "Cleared rung 15, the format of the Japanese 1st-kyu mental exam."
"1st dan, since she is past every kyu grade."
"Top of the ladder: a certified mental math expert."
"1st kyu on the Japanese mental exam ladder."

questions.text: At pickup, a dad asks, "If I get certified, could I quit my job and teach this full time?" What may you say?

options.label: "Plenty of instructors make $2,000 a month part time, so it's realistic."
"Yes. A few full classes a week pays more than most office jobs, once word gets around."
"Sure. Most instructors earn back the course fee in the first month."
"Most instructors land between $20 and $40 a session. Your rates are yours to set."

questions.text: During class, a mom at the back whispers answers to her son. What do you do?

options.label: Ask her to wait outside in the car until class is over, so her son can think for himself.
Give her your rule: hands in her lap, no answers. Hand her the one line for the stage.
Let it go. A parent who helps is a good thing.
Seat her beside him, so she can check each of his answers as he goes.

questions.text: A Stage 4 girl moves from 1-digit to 2-digit mental sums. Her answers slow way down. What do you do?

options.label: Make the rounds shorter for now, so the new sums feel easier and she keeps her confidence.
Go back to 1-digit sums for a month, and then try the 2-digit sums again.
Expect a slow week. Keep the rounds the same size, and slow the beat.
Speed up the beat, so that she has no time left to say the numbers in words.

questions.text: A mom asks, "Can I drop him at your house for a private lesson while I run errands?" What do you say?

options.label: "Yes. Just leave your number, and text me when you're on your way back."
"Please stay. A parent stays in the room, and I'm never alone with one child."
"Sure. He'll focus much better without you in the room, and you'll get a free hour."
"Yes, as long as you're back within the hour."

questions.text: A dad says, "She comes to your class every Saturday. So we skip practice at home." What do you say?

options.label: "Class is where she learns the move. The fifteen minutes at home is where it becomes automatic."
"Practice at home only in the week before a boss."
"That's fine. One good class a week is enough at this stage."
"Then do two hours at home on Sundays to catch up."

questions.text: You run a first flash round at the table: "Three." "Five." "One." The child says, "Nine." What do you say?

options.label: "Yes." Then the next round.
"Amazing! You're a genius!"
"Right! Now tell me the numbers I said."
"Are you sure? Check it on the beads."

questions.text: A Stage 1 boy reads a rod as 7. Its heaven bead sits up, away from the beam. Two earth beads touch the beam. What do you say?

options.label: "No, it's 2. Next one."
"A bead only counts when it touches the beam."
"Count every bead on the rod, from the top down to the bottom."
"Let me clear it and set it for you."

questions.text: A Stage 6 boy needs five seconds for 7 × 8. His first multiply lesson is next. What do you do?

options.label: Let him keep a times-table chart next to his abacus.
Skip ahead to division, since it uses fewer facts.
Start multiplying on the beads. The facts will come with practice.
Put the times-table lesson in his daily quest until he passes it three days in a row.

questions.text: A mom asks, "Will the beads help him remember his spelling words?" What do you say?

options.label: "It boosts memory and attention, so his spelling should get better too."
"Most parents tell me school gets easier all round, so I would expect it."
"Trials found gains in arithmetic, and in the visual memory that holds the beads. Not in general memory, so I can't promise spelling."
"Yes. Abacus kids remember more of everything, spelling included, within a few months of practice."

questions.text: A dad says, "Her gifted test is in the spring. Will this raise her IQ by then?" What do you say?

options.label: "Yes. Abacus kids score higher on IQ tests, and with daily practice she has plenty of time before spring."
"If she practices an hour a day instead of fifteen minutes, it should lift her score in time."
"It won't change her IQ, but it will boost her memory and focus."
"No study has found an IQ gain, so I won't promise one. Trials found faster, more accurate arithmetic."

questions.text: A Stage 2 girl works 43 + 4 and writes 42. What do you say?

options.label: Say "It's 47," and go straight on to the next problem.
Ask "Free beads, or friend?" about the ones rod.
Ask "Where did the ten come from?" and wait for her answer.
Say "Finger under the line you're on," and have her redo it.

questions.text: Ten minutes into a drill, a boy starts to cry over a take-away. What do you do?

options.label: Stop warmly: "We're done for today. Good work. Same time tomorrow."
Give him the answers, so the day ends on a win.
Tell him that crying won't fix the beads.
Finish the drill first, so he learns that we push through the hard moments.

questions.text: Maya takes the Apprentice boss. Parts two and three pass. Part one, the single carries and borrows, scores 7 of 10. Which message do you send her parent?

options.label: "Not yet. Part one, the single carries and borrows, is next. We'll go back to the big-friend lessons and try again Saturday."
"Maya isn't ready for Stage 3 yet. We'll start again from Stage 1 next week."
"Unfortunately, Maya failed the boss this time. We'll give it another go soon."
"Maya failed part one, but parts two and three were great. Well done to her."

questions.text: A mom looks at the Bead Score chart. Her son's line sits below the shaded band for age nine. His line has climbed on every test. She asks, "Is he behind?" What do you say?

options.label: "Try not to look at the chart. It only causes stress."
"The bands come from thousands of children, so it's worth a little worry."
"The bands are estimates, not a measured sample. His own line is the honest number, and it keeps climbing."
"Yes. Most nine-year-olds in the program score higher than he does, so we'll add a second session each day."

questions.text: Another instructor wants to post, "Teach abacus from home and earn $3,000 a month!" What do you tell her?

options.label: Lower it to $1,000 a month, so it sounds more real to parents.
Keep it. How she runs her business and her posts is up to her.
Keep it, and add "results may vary" in small print at the bottom.
Cut the figure. Use only "Most instructors land between $20 and $40 a session. Your rates are yours to set."

questions.text: During the written drill, a girl keeps looking at her neighbor's beads. What do you change?

options.label: Seat the kids so no one can see another child's abacus during written drills.
Nothing. She learns a lot by watching a faster child, and she'll stop on her own.
Pair her with that neighbor, so the two of them can work out each problem together.
Tell the class that copying is cheating, and take a point off her score each time.

questions.text: During a mental round, a boy's fingers twitch on the table. What do you do?

options.label: Give him the abacus back until the twitching stops.
Let them move. They're part of the picture.
Tell him that moving his fingers is cheating.
Ask him to sit on his hands, so the picture does the work.

questions.text: You log on for an online lesson. The child is home alone. Her mom will be back in an hour. What do you do?

options.label: Start, but keep the call short, about fifteen minutes, and end before she gets bored.
Start, with your own camera off, so she can relax.
Don't start. Online, a parent stays in the room with the camera on. Set a new time.
Start. Online there is nothing to worry about, since you're not in the same room.

questions.text: A mom says, "We're busy on weekdays. So we do one hour of beads every Sunday." What do you say?

options.label: "Skip home practice, and just come to class."
"Great. More minutes at once means more progress."
"Fifteen minutes a day works better. Short, daily reps build the picture, and tired ones don't."
"Make it two hours on Sunday, to cover the whole week."

questions.text: You read a dictation round. The next number is minus eighteen. How do you say it?

options.label: "Minus," then a short pause, then "eighteen," so she hears both parts.
"Minus eighteen," as one chunk, on the beat.
"Minus one, eight," one digit at a time.
"Eighteen," then "take it away."

questions.text: The rod shows 3. A girl adds 2. She brings the five down, then takes away two. The rod shows 6. What do you ask?

options.label: "What's the friend of two?"
"Can you take away three instead?"
"Can you count up from three on your fingers?"
"Where did the ten come from?"

questions.text: In 2,752 ÷ 32, a girl's first guess is 9. It is too big, and she freezes. What do you say?

options.label: "Let's switch to an easier problem."
"Wrong. The first digit is 8."
"You need to estimate better. Start again from the top."
"Too big? Lower it by one, and try again."

questions.text: You are making a flyer for your first class. Which headline may you use?

options.label: "Boost your child's memory and focus in just fifteen minutes a day."
"Works for every child. Better grades, guaranteed."
"Raise your child's IQ. See the results in two weeks."
"Fifteen minutes a day. Your child learns to add and take away on the beads, then in their head."

questions.text: You are writing your two-minute parent talk. Your nephew has ADHD, and the beads helped him love math. How do you tell it?

options.label: Tell what happened, true and plain. Never say the beads treat ADHD.
Say the beads fixed his ADHD. It is his true story, so it's fine to say.
Say that most kids with ADHD do better with the beads.
Leave out the ADHD, and say he was always a top student.

questions.text: A Stage 3 girl works 51 − 3 and writes 58. What do you say?

options.label: "Take away the friend, then carry one to the left."
"What's the friend of three? Say it, then do the move again."
"Add the friend, then borrow one from the left."
"It's 48. Let's just do the next one together."

questions.text: A Stage 3 boy starts every problem on the ones rod. What do you say?

options.label: Explain how the mental picture fills in from the big place down.
Let him use the school way, since it is what he knows.
"Left to right," and nothing else.
Nothing. The answer comes out the same either way.

questions.text: A girl passes the Adept boss. But she still counts beads one at a time, and the beads make her anxious. What do you do?

options.label: Have her take the Adept boss again until she passes it twice.
Keep her in Adept and repeat the drills. It costs a week. Moving up too early costs a stage.
Open the next stage, and add fifteen more minutes a day.
Open the next stage. A pass is a pass.

questions.text: A mom says, "I read online that the abacus doesn't really work. Is any of this proven?" What do you say?

options.label: "Yes. Studies in India and China proved it raises IQ and memory."
"The research doesn't matter much. Just watch what your child can do in a month."
"Every study agrees it works for all kids, so don't worry about what you read."
"Some trials found real gains in arithmetic. None found an IQ gain. One US trial with first graders found no benefit."

questions.text: You ask a friend to help teach your class. She asks how much she could make if she gets certified too. What may you say?

options.label: "You'll earn back the whole course fee in your first month, and after that it's all profit."
"Most instructors land between $20 and $40 a session. Your rates are yours to set."
"As much as you want. Parents are lining up for this."
"Four classes a week covers a car payment, easy."

questions.text: In your class, one boy shouts every answer before the others finish. What do you change?

options.label: Use whiteboards or hands up. Say the rule once: "Answers at the end, on your board."
Send him out to the hall for the rest of the round.
Let him. His speed pushes the others to keep up.
Move him to the front of the room, so he can lead the group and set the pace for the others.

questions.text: You make up a mental round for a Stage 2 child: 4, then 3, then 2. What is wrong with it?

options.label: Nothing. She knows small friends on the beads by now, so her head can use them too.
It is too short. Stage 2 mental rounds need at least five numbers to count.
Adding 3 to 4 needs a small friend. Stage 2 mental rounds use free beads only.
Nothing is wrong, as long as you read it at a steady beat of one number a second.

questions.text: Class is over. One girl's ride is late, and the other families have gone. What do you do?

options.label: Drive her home yourself, so she isn't late.
Let her wait outside on her own, since class is over.
Close the door and do extra drills with her while you wait, so the time isn't wasted.
Wait with her in the main room with the door open, and call her parent.

questions.text: A girl's Bead Score comes in two rungs lower than last month. She took it at bedtime, tired. What do you do?

options.label: Move her back a stage until the score comes back up to where it was.
Test her again every night this week until the score climbs back.
Tell her parents she is slipping behind, so they can add practice.
Treat it as a tired test. Do a normal two weeks, then retake it.

questions.text: A dad says his Stage 5 son will show flash rounds at a family dinner. Grandpa plans to go fast and throw in a big number. What do you tell the dad?

options.label: "Fine, but give him the abacus, so it's fair."
"Let him. One rule: one number at a time, said once."
"Fine. And repeat any number he asks for."
"Don't. Only his instructor should give flash rounds."

questions.text: A Stage 3 boy says, "Carrying is too slow. I want to quit." What do you do this week?

options.label: Promise him a prize if he finishes the stage.
Skip him ahead to Stage 4, so it feels new.
Shorten the session, or drop to the daily quest alone. No speech, and no bargain.
Give a short talk on why quitters never win.

questions.text: A boy works 952 ÷ 7. His answer comes out as 1,360, ten times too big. What do you have him do?

options.label: Point to the rod where each quotient digit goes, before he places it.
Divide from right to left from now on, the same way he learned it at school.
Check each answer with a calculator before he writes it down.
Work only problems with no zeros in them for a week or two.

questions.text: A grandma says, "My granddaughter hates math. Will this work for her?" What do you say?

options.label: "Probably not. Some kids just aren't math kids, and that's fine."
"I can't promise it works for every child. Each child moves at her own pace, and the ladder shows where she is."
"She'll love math within a week. They all do, once they see the beads."
"Yes. It works for every child who sticks with it, whatever they think of math."
